why.support: Your words show how you feel about someone. The right **tone** helps you get what you need.
why.core: The words you choose show how you see someone — and change how they see you. Get the **tone** right and you get the shift swap, the extension, the second chance.
why.extend: Every message signals a relationship. The words, greeting and tone you choose position you — as a mate, a professional, a customer. Choosing them on purpose is how you get taken seriously.

articles.title: Turn it up, turn it down

body.support:
Think of your words like a **volume dial**.

With mates, you turn it **down**. Short words. Slang. Emojis. That's **casual**.

With a boss or teacher, you turn it **up**. Full words. A greeting. Please and thanks. That's **formal**.

Ask yourself three questions:

1. **Who** is it for?
2. **Why** am I writing?
3. **Where** will they read it?

The more someone is in charge, the more **formal** you go.

Short replies count too. A 👍 can mean “yes”.

Before you send, read it again. Fix mistakes.
body.core:
Think of your words like a **volume dial**. With your mates, you turn it down: short, relaxed, full of in-jokes and emojis. That's **casual** language. With a boss, a teacher or a stranger at a service desk, you turn it up: full words, a greeting, please and thanks. That's **formal** language.

Neither one is wrong. The trick is choosing the right one. Ask yourself three questions:

1. **Who** am I talking to? How well do I know them? Are they in charge?
2. **Why** am I writing? Am I asking for something, saying sorry, or giving information?
3. **Where** will they read it? A text, an email, a phone call?

The less well you know someone, and the more they have a say over you, the more **formal** you go. A message to your boss about a shift should have a greeting, full words, a clear request and your name at the end.

One more thing: short replies count. An emoji or a quick “ok” can be taken as a real answer — so think before you send.

Before you hit send, **proofread**. Read it once more, out loud if you can. Fix spelling, add a greeting, and check it says what you mean.
body.extend:
Think of your words like a **volume dial**. With your mates, you turn it down: short, relaxed, full of in-jokes and emojis. That's **casual** language. With a boss, a teacher or a stranger at a service desk, you turn it up: full words, a greeting, please and thanks. That's **formal** language.

Neither one is wrong. The trick is choosing the right one. Ask yourself three questions:

1. **Who** am I talking to? How well do I know them? Are they in charge?
2. **Why** am I writing? Am I asking for something, saying sorry, or giving information?
3. **Where** will they read it? A text, an email, a phone call?

The less well you know someone, and the more they have a say over you, the more **formal** you go. Linguists call this choice your **register**.

Your language also shows who you are. Slang can show you belong to a group; formal language can show you're reliable and serious. Switching between them isn't being fake — it's a skill.

Short replies count. An emoji or a quick “ok” can be taken as a real answer — so think before you send. And before you hit send, **proofread**: cut anything repeated, put the most important point first, and check every word.

caseStudies.title: The 👍 that cost $82,000

body.support:
A grain buyer in Canada texted a farmer a contract. He wrote: “Please confirm flax contract.”

The farmer replied with just a **👍**.

Later, there was a fight about the deal. The farmer said 👍 meant “I got your message”. The buyer said it meant “I agree”.

In 2023 a judge said the 👍 meant **“I agree”**. The farmer had to pay about **$82,000**.

At work, even a tiny reply can count.
body.core:
In 2021, a grain buyer in Canada texted a farmer. He sent a photo of a contract to buy flax. He wrote: “Please confirm flax contract.” The farmer replied with one thing: a **👍 thumbs-up emoji**.

When the flax wasn't delivered, the buyer went to court. The farmer said the thumbs-up only meant he had **received** the message — not that he agreed.

In 2023 a judge ruled that the 👍 **did** mean “I agree”. The farmer was ordered to pay about **$82,000** (Canadian). In 2024, Saskatchewan's Court of Appeal upheld the decision.

The lesson: at work, even a tiny reply can be taken seriously.

teacher.overview: Students learn that language choices depend on **who** they're writing to, **why**, and **where** — and practise turning the “volume” of formality up and down. The core literacy is selecting language for social context and relationships, then creating and editing a short formal message. It's high-relevance for students with part-time jobs or about to start one.
prep: Collect two or three real (anonymised) messages students might send a boss — or use the examples in the workbook.
Have the explainer ready on the board.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The volume dial
steps: **Hook (5 min):** project “cant come fri lol” — would you send this to your boss? Why not?
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** casual vs formal; model Who? Why? Where? with three versions of one message.
**Exit:** one casual and one formal way to say “I'm running late”.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Sort and switch
steps: **Read (15 min):** “Turn it up, turn it down” + Check your reading.
**Model then independent (20 min):** Turn it up table.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Anatomy and a real case
steps: **Explicit teaching (15 min):** label the email anatomy together.
**Case study (20 min):** the 👍 contract; discuss what it means for work messages.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Write it, fix it
steps: **Model (10 min):** draft a request on the board, then edit it aloud using the checklist.
**Write (25 min):** final mission. Fast finishers: Level Up edit.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

keyPoints: Who? Why? Where? decide how formal to be.
More formal: greeting with name, full words, clear polite request, sign-off.
Short replies and emojis can be taken as real answers.
Always re-read and fix before sending.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** Who? Why? Where? Casual = short, slang, emojis; formal = greeting, full words, please/thanks, sign-off. Short replies can be taken as agreement.

**Casual or formal?** omw — Casual. Ms Rossi email — Formal. Sick message to Sam — Formal. lol same — Casual. “Thanks for the info” — Depends. “To whom it may concern” — Formal.

**Email anatomy:** 1 recipient; 2 subject; 3 greeting; 4 opening; 5 reason; 6 request; 7 sign-off.

**Case study:** 👍 — the judge decided it meant “I agree”; ordered to pay about $82,000 (Canadian); upheld on appeal in 2024.
